result.summary: Hercules shoots the centaur Nessus for trying to carry off Deïanira, and the dying Nessus gives her his blood-soaked tunic as a false love charm. Hearing a rumour about Iole, Deïanira sends the tunic to Hercules, who is tortured by its poison, hurls Lichas into the sea, and burns himself on a pyre on Œta. Jupiter then takes his immortal part up to the stars.

scenes.title: Book's argument for the fable
scenes.summary: A prose summary outlines the story of Nessus, the tunic, the death of Hercules and his deification.

scenes.title: Nessus at the river Evenus
scenes.summary: Hercules entrusts Deïanira to Nessus at the flooded river, then shoots the centaur as he flees with her. Nessus dies after giving Deïanira his bloody garment as a supposed love charm.
scenes.stakes: Deïanira is in danger of abduction; Nessus risks death at Hercules' hands.

scenes.title: Deïanira sends the tunic
scenes.summary: Rumour tells Deïanira that Hercules loves Iole. After wavering, she sends the tunic by Lichas.
scenes.stakes: Deïanira fears losing her husband's love and her place in his bed.

scenes.title: Torment of Hercules on Œta
scenes.summary: The poison burns Hercules as he sacrifices. He laments his labours, curses Juno, and hurls Lichas into the sea, where he becomes a rock.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces agonizing death from the poison.

scenes.title: Pyre and apotheosis
scenes.summary: Hercules lies on the pyre lit by Philoctetes. Jupiter calms the gods, and Hercules' mortal part burns away as Jupiter carries him to the stars.
scenes.stakes: Hercules' mortal body is consumed; he stands to gain immortality.

notable_quotes.reason: Nessus's dying vengeance sets the tragedy in motion.
Hercules' bitter cry doubting the gods' existence.

analysis.text: A well-meant act of jealous love becomes the instrument of destruction, and the hero who survived every labour is undone by a gift.
Death burns away Hercules' mortal part, so suffering leads to apotheosis.

legacy.text: The story inspired Sophocles' Trachiniae and Seneca's Hercules Oetaeus; 'shirt of Nessus' became a phrase for a fatal gift.

fun_facts.text: The 'shirt of Nessus' idiom is used in European languages for a poisoned or fatal legacy.

language_notes.text: Alcides is a name for Hercules, after his grandfather Alcaeus. Aonian (Theban, from Aonia in Boeotia) and Calydonian (from Calydon, Deïanira's home) are likewise descriptive names.
The spoil of the lion is the pelt of the Nemean lion, another of his labours, which Hercules wore as a cloak.
Ravisher here means abductor, one who carries a woman off by force, not necessarily a rapist in the modern sense.
Nessus is a Centaur, son of Ixion, who was bound to a revolving wheel in the underworld for trying to seduce Juno. Hercules reminds Nessus of that punishment.
The arrows were tipped with the venom of the Lernæan Hydra, the many-headed serpent Hercules killed in one of his labours.
Son of Amphitryon is Hercules; Amphitryon was his mortal stepfather, while Jupiter was his true father. Iole was a princess of Œchalia, whom Hercules had just conquered.
Contrivance means a clever scheme or plan.
Meleager, Deïanira's brother, was a hero of Calydon. The appeal to him recalls her family's fierce, violent temper.
Nessus was a centaur Hercules killed with a poisoned arrow. Dying, he falsely told Deïanira his blood would work as a love charm.
The Lernæan Echidna means the Hydra of Lerna, whose venom Hercules had put on his arrows. Nessus's blood was tainted with it.
Daughter of Saturn is Juno, Hercules' persecutor, who set his labours. Saturn was Jupiter's father, so Juno is Jupiter's sister and wife.
Ironic: 'becomes' means 'is fitting for'. A stepmother, Juno, would be expected to grant a cruel favour such as his death.
The Iberian shepherd is Geryon, the three-bodied giant whose cattle Hercules took. Cerberus is the three-headed hound of the underworld.
Refers to the belt of the Amazon queen Hippolyte, and to the golden apples of the Hesperides guarded by a dragon.
The Hydra was a many-headed serpent whose severed heads grew back doubled, until Hercules burned the stumps.
The Thracian steeds are the man-eating mares of Diomedes; Hercules killed Diomedes and fed him to them.
Eurystheus was the king who imposed the twelve labours on Hercules at Juno's urging; Hercules resents that he lives on.
Alcides is a name for Hercules, from his grandfather Alcaeus.
Philoctetes, son of Pœas, receives Hercules' bow as reward for lighting the pyre. The arrows are fated to be needed again at Troy.
"Saturnian Jupiter" means Jupiter, son of Saturn; the epithet identifies his parentage.
His mother is Alcmena, a mortal woman; Hercules' mortal half comes from her, his divine half from Jupiter.
The doubled "if any one" hints at Juno, who hated Hercules as the child of Jupiter's affair.
Mulciber is a name for Vulcan, god of fire, here standing for fire itself.
"Slough" is the shed skin of a snake; "instinct with" means filled with.

context_notes.text: This is the treacherous gift that will drive the plot: the poisoned tunic becomes the instrument of Hercules' death.
The flooded river explains why Hercules needs a Centaur's help, since Centaurs were known for their strength and speed.
Cenæan Jupiter was worshipped at Cenæum, a cape on Euboea. Hercules was preparing a thanksgiving sacrifice there.
Lichas was Hercules' attendant and herald, used here as an innocent messenger.
Busiris was an Egyptian king who sacrificed strangers; Hercules killed him when he tried to sacrifice him.
Antæus, a giant, drew strength from his mother Earth; Hercules lifted him off the ground and crushed him.
Hercules briefly held up the sky for Atlas while Atlas fetched the golden apples.
Lichas was Hercules' attendant who brought him the poisoned robe sent by Deianira, unaware of its nature.
Hercules is dying from the poisoned shirt of Nessus, sent by his wife Deianira, and so builds his own pyre on Mount Œta.
The "royal spouse" is Juno, Hercules' lifelong persecutor, who resents his deification.
The Tirynthian hero is Hercules, named for Tiryns, the city linked with his upbringing.

literary_notes.text: The narrator suddenly addresses Nessus directly as 'thee', adding emotion and foreshadowing his punishment for desire.
Hercules turns Nessus' speed into a joke: the wound will catch him instead of Hercules' feet.
Nessus' vow of revenge and the 'incentive to love' gift hint at the disaster that will destroy Hercules.
Rumour acts as a living being who delights in lies and grows with each telling, showing how gossip spreads.
She addresses her absent brother Meleager, which shows her emotional turmoil and her wish for a violent family precedent.
The reader knows the gift is deadly, while Deïanira and Lichas do not, so her gentle words and good intent become tragic.
Calling the tunic venom signals Hercules' coming agony and death, though he receives it unaware.
The hissing blood is compared to hot metal quenched in water, making the poison's heat vivid and physical.
A run of questions recounting his labours builds bitter indignation at his reward; the series continues to sentence 54.
The hero who served the gods now doubts they exist, a bitter reversal of his lifetime of labour.
Hercules is likened to a wounded tiger fleeing with spears in its body, showing his agony and wild rage.
The hailstone-formation comparison explains Lichas' petrification step by step, lending a natural process to the miracle.
The narrator suddenly addresses Hercules as "thou", making his calm on the pyre vivid and heroic.
Hercules' expression is compared to that of a feasting guest, stressing his contempt for pain.
The flames roar and "reach" the limbs as if they were hostile, yet they are despised by him.
Jupiter's veiled warning to Juno is sharp: even a reluctant god must approve what is deserved.
Hercules shedding his mortal body is likened to a snake's renewal, showing rebirth into a grander form.
